title: The Fare Hike
subtitle: A forty percent fare rise brings commuters to the depot at dawn
coldOpen: 05:30. New fare boards go up: forty percent more from today.
06:15. Commuters sit on the depot exit; no bus leaves.
The transit chief announced it by notice, not by meeting.

briefing.grievance: Daily-wage commuters cannot absorb a forty percent rise announced overnight. They want the rise withdrawn or phased, and they want to be asked before, not told after.
knownFacts: The authority is running a deficit; fuel costs rose 30% this year.
The rise was approved by the board without public notice.
Sixty buses serve two lakh passengers from this depot daily.
unverifiedClaims: A post says the board gave itself a bonus the same day.
A message says private operators paid for the rise to push riders to their vans.
briefing.responsibility: You run the transit authority and the depot policing. The deficit is real, the rise was clumsy, and the sit-in is lawful.
briefing.objective: Get buses moving by agreement, open the books on the rise, and give riders a say before the next one.

decisions.title: No bus leaves
decisions.situation: Three hundred commuters are seated across the depot exit. Two lakh people are waiting at stops. The chief wants police to open the gate.

options.title: Pause the rise; publish the accounts
options.preview: Old fares today; the deficit figures go up on the depot wall.
options.authority: Duty of candour: say what is known and what is not
options.consequence: The sit-in has what it asked for: time and numbers. Buses roll.

options.title: Meet the commuter association at the gate
options.preview: You hear the demand and agree a talks timetable; the gate opens one lane.
options.authority: Duty to hear grievances; Article 19(1)(a) free expression
options.consequence: The association opens a lane itself once a meeting is set.

options.title: Clear the exit with police
options.preview: Officers carry seated commuters off the road.
options.authority: Article 19(2)–(3): restrictions must be reasonable and specific
options.consequence: Buses leave over the people who ride them. Tomorrow’s sit-in is bigger.

delayed.message: The crackdown hardens people who had stayed out of it. More arrive, angrier.

options.title: Hold the buses inside
options.preview: No talks, no pause; the city walks to work.
options.consequence: Two lakh people are late and angry at you, not at the rise.

options.authority: Due process: establish the facts before acting on them
options.consequence: The sabotage has faces. The sit-in does not get the blame.

decisions.title: The private vans
decisions.situation: Private vans are charging triple at the stops. A councillor wants the depot cleared. The association offers to run a minimum service itself.

rightsMoments.question: Commuters are sitting across a bus depot exit over a fare rise. Can their association be banned as an unlawful body?

options.text: No. Peaceful association and assembly are protected; obstruction is addressed by proportionate, specific measures, not by banning the group.
options.feedback: Correct. The right to associate survives a sit-in; the remedy is proportionate policing and negotiation.

options.text: Yes. Blocking an essential service forfeits the right to associate.
options.feedback: Obstruction can be addressed, but a ban on the association is disproportionate and silences the people you must negotiate with.

options.text: Yes, if the board votes for it.
options.feedback: A board vote cannot override constitutional protections for association.

rightsMoments.principle: Article 19(1)(c) protects the right to form associations; restrictions must be reasonable and specific. A sit-in is answered by proportionate steps and dialogue, not by outlawing the group.
rightsMoments.why: The association ended up running the minimum service; banning it would have removed the only partner the authority had.

simple.question: Commuters sit across a bus depot exit. Can their group be banned?

options.a: No. People may form groups and protest peacefully. Deal with the block fairly.
options.b: Yes. Blocking buses ends the right to form groups.
options.c: Yes, if the board votes for it.

feedback.a: Yes! Handle the block fairly. Do not ban the group.
feedback.b: No. Banning the group is too much and leaves nobody to talk to.
feedback.c: A board vote cannot cancel a constitutional right.

simple.principle: People may form groups and protest peacefully. Answer a block with fair steps and talks, not a ban.
simple.why: The riders’ group ended up running the buses. Banning it would have removed your only partner.
